concept.title: Cell Address, Cell References, Relative Reference, Absolute Reference, Mixed Reference

body.text: A cell is the intersection of a row and a column. Every cell has a unique address called a Cell Reference. Excel uses cell references in formulas instead of typing actual values. This makes formulas dynamic because they automatically update when the data changes.

body.code:
Formula in C1:

=A1+B1

A1 and B1 are cell references.

body.text: Cell references make formulas flexible. If the value in a referenced cell changes, Excel automatically recalculates the result.
Excel provides three types of cell references: Relative, Absolute, and Mixed references.

rows: Either row or column remains fixed

body.text: A Relative Reference changes automatically when a formula is copied to another cell. This is the default reference type used by Excel.

body.text: An Absolute Reference keeps a cell fixed when a formula is copied. Use the dollar sign ($) before the column, row, or both to lock the reference.
Suppose F1 contains the GST rate (18%). When the formula =B2*$F$1 is copied down, B2 changes to B3, B4, and so on, but $F$1 always remains fixed.
A Mixed Reference locks either the row or the column, but not both. It is useful when copying formulas across rows and columns.
Mixed references are commonly used in multiplication tables, price lists, and matrix calculations.
While editing a formula, place the cursor on the cell reference and press the F4 key to cycle through the different reference types.
Shortcut: Select a cell reference inside a formula and press F4 to quickly add or remove the $ symbol.
